items.stem: Distinguish between the Annales approach and Marxist history.
items.answer: Marxist history stresses class struggle and economic change; the Annales school stresses long-term geographical, social and mental structures without a single theory of class.

items.stem: "Revisionist historians are those who deny that events happened." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: In historiography, revisionism means reinterpreting the past; denial (e.g. Holocaust denial) is a distortion of evidence, not legitimate revisionism.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Fischer controversy of the 1960s and explain what it reveals about revisionism in historiography.
items.answer: Fritz Fischer’s argument that Germany sought world power in 1914 challenged the West German consensus and provoked bitter debate. It shows how new archival evidence and a new generation’s perspective can overturn an orthodox view.

items.answer: Value: A founding statement of modern source-based history. Limitations: It expresses an ideal; Ranke’s own work focused on states and elites and reflected his conservative views.

items.markingKey: Browning argues that ordinary men killed because of conformity, careerism and wartime brutalisation; Goldhagen argues they killed because of a uniquely German eliminationist antisemitism. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between history and memory.
items.answer: History is a critical, evidence-based reconstruction of the past; memory is a selective, emotional and identity-based recollection that can be shaped by politics.
items.markingKey: History is a critical, evidence-based reconstruction of the past; memory is a selective, emotional and identity-based recollection that can be shaped by politics. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that Ranke’s approach shows that history can be completely objective. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Ranke aimed for source-based accuracy, but his choice of subjects (states, diplomacy) reflected his own assumptions.
items.markingKey: Ranke aimed for source-based accuracy, but his choice of subjects (states, diplomacy) reflected his own assumptions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Source B: Daniel Goldhagen, US political scientist, Hitler’s Willing Executioners: Ordinary Germans and the Holocaust, 1996 (adapted)

The perpetrators were ordinary Germans animated by antisemitism, by a particular type of antisemitism that led them to conclude that the Jews ought to die.

How far can Source B be trusted as evidence for the motives of Holocaust perpetrators? Refer to the origin, purpose and content of the source.
items.answer: Value: A bold, much-debated thesis that drew attention to perpetrators’ beliefs. Limitations: Widely criticised for selective use of evidence and for a mono-causal, national-character explanation; written as a provocative revision of Browning.
items.markingKey: Value: A bold, much-debated thesis that drew attention to perpetrators’ beliefs. Limitations: Widely criticised for selective use of evidence and for a mono-causal, national-character explanation; written as a provocative revision of Browning. Award up to [3]: the response must refer to origin, purpose and content and link each to value or limitation for the stated enquiry; at least one value and one limitation are needed for full marks; a list of features without explaining their effect on value is capped at half marks.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Murambi Genocide Memorial and explain what it reveals about the politics of genocide commemoration.
items.answer: At a former technical school where tens of thousands were killed in April 1994, preserved bodies are displayed. Displaying remains forces confrontation with the genocide but raises ethical questions and serves the state’s narrative.
items.markingKey: Context (At a former technical school where tens of thousands were killed in April 1994, preserved bodies are displayed.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Displaying remains forces confrontation with the genocide but raises ethical questions and serves the state’s narrative. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the politics of genocide commemoration.

items.stem:
Source B: Leopold von Ranke, German historian, preface to Histories of the Latin and Germanic Nations from 1494 to 1514, 1824 (translation)

To history has been given the function of judging the past, of instructing men for the profit of future years. The present attempt does not aspire to such high offices. It wants only to show what actually happened.

What does Source B suggest about different approaches to writing history? Refer closely to the source in your answer.
items.answer: History should not judge or teach lessons but should simply show what happened.
items.markingKey: History should not judge or teach lessons but should simply show what happened. Award 1 mark for each relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]. Points must come from the source itself; own knowledge is not credited in this question.

items.stem:
Source C: Paraphrased from Christopher Browning, US historian, Ordinary Men: Reserve Police Battalion 101 and the Final Solution in Poland, 1992

The men of Reserve Police Battalion 101 were not chosen for their ideological commitment. Most killed not out of hatred but because they did not want to break ranks, to appear weak or to leave the dirty work to their comrades.

With reference to its origin, purpose and content, analyse the value and limitations of Source C for an historian studying the motives of Holocaust perpetrators.
items.answer: Value: Based on post-war judicial interrogations of 125 battalion members, it provides detailed evidence. Limitations: The testimony was given in self-defence to prosecutors, so men may have minimised antisemitism; the battalion may not be typical.
items.markingKey: Value: Based on post-war judicial interrogations of 125 battalion members, it provides detailed evidence. Limitations: The testimony was given in self-defence to prosecutors, so men may have minimised antisemitism; the battalion may not be typical. items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from Paul Kagame, President of Rwanda, speech at the 20th commemoration of the genocide (Kwibuka 20), Kigali, 7 April 2014

Remembrance is not only about the past. We remember to ensure that such a thing never happens again, and to build a Rwanda in which we are all Rwandans.

How far can Source A be trusted as evidence for history, memory and commemoration of genocide? Refer to the origin, purpose and content of the source.
items.answer: Value: A speech by the head of state at the major commemoration, showing the official purpose of memory. Limitations: It presents the government’s narrative and political aims; it does not address criticisms about RPF crimes or restrictions on debate.

items.stem:
Source A: Leopold von Ranke, German historian, preface to Histories of the Latin and Germanic Nations from 1494 to 1514, 1824 (translation)

To history has been given the function of judging the past, of instructing men for the profit of future years. The present attempt does not aspire to such high offices. It wants only to show what actually happened.

Source B: E. P. Thompson, British Marxist historian, preface to The Making of the English Working Class, 1963 (extract)

I am seeking to rescue the poor stockinger, the Luddite cropper, the “obsolete” hand-loom weaver, the “utopian” artisan from the enormous condescension of posterity.

“Marxist historiography has made the most important contribution to historical understanding.” Using Sources A and B and your own knowledge, how far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Marxism transformed social history, but no single school has a monopoly on insight.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – supporting: history from below; economic and social explanations of revolutions; Hobsbawm’s Age of trilogy. Challenging: determinism and neglect of individuals; Annales and cultural history; decline after 1989. Judgement: Marxism transformed social history, but no single school has a monopoly on insight. Candidates must use both sources and their own knowledge; Markbands – 6–8: focused response; effective use of the sources and accurate own knowledge, integrated (synthesised) to support a clear, balanced judgement; 4–5: some focus on the question; uses sources or own knowledge, with some analysis but little synthesis; 1–3: limited understanding; generalised comments, sources or own knowledge used descriptively; 0: does not reach the standard of the descriptors below.

items.stem:
Source A: Paraphrased from Christopher Browning, US historian, Ordinary Men: Reserve Police Battalion 101 and the Final Solution in Poland, 1992

The men of Reserve Police Battalion 101 were not chosen for their ideological commitment. Most killed not out of hatred but because they did not want to break ranks, to appear weak or to leave the dirty work to their comrades.

Source B: Daniel Goldhagen, US political scientist, Hitler’s Willing Executioners: Ordinary Germans and the Holocaust, 1996 (adapted)

The perpetrators were ordinary Germans animated by antisemitism, by a particular type of antisemitism that led them to conclude that the Jews ought to die.

Compare and contrast what Sources A and B reveal about the motives of Holocaust perpetrators.
items.answer: Both study ordinary German perpetrators, partly the same battalion. Browning explains killing through conformity and situational pressures, whereas Goldhagen explains it through deep-rooted antisemitism; Browning’s explanation is situational and universal, Goldhagen’s ideological and specifically German.
items.markingKey: Both study ordinary German perpetrators, partly the same battalion. Browning explains killing through conformity and situational pressures, whereas Goldhagen explains it through deep-rooted antisemitism; Browning’s explanation is situational and universal, Goldhagen’s ideological and specifically German. Award 1 mark per valid, explicitly linked point of comparison or contrast, up to [6]; at least one comparison and one contrast are needed for full marks. A running (integrated) comparison is preferred to end-on description; do not credit points about provenance in this question.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that official commemoration of genocide does more to serve political purposes than to preserve historical truth?
items.answer: Commemoration serves both truth and politics; historians must analyse memorials as sources of both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Rwandan state narrative and genocide ideology law; Serbian commemoration of NATO bombing; selective memory. Arguments against: memorials preserve evidence and honour victims; educate against denial; survivors’ testimony. Supported judgement: Commemoration serves both truth and politics; historians must analyse memorials as sources of both. Markbands: Use the IB Paper 2/3 markbands, scaled to the marks: top band – clearly focused, well structured, accurate and relevant knowledge used to support critical analysis, different perspectives evaluated, reasoned conclusion; middle band – mostly accurate knowledge, some analysis but partly narrative; lower band – little understanding of the demands, mainly description.
